authorities.name: Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), s.223(1)
authorities.date_note: Enactment year, following the High Court's 1992 Mabo (No 2) decision. The compilation the researching agent read was registered 12 June 2024 (C2024C00224). This session's own re-fetch could not independently confirm the current wording due to the document's size, not an access block.
authorities.proposition: 'Native title' or 'native title rights and interests' means the communal, group or individual rights and interests of Aboriginal peoples or Torres Strait Islanders in relation to land or waters, where the rights and interests are possessed under the traditional laws acknowledged, and traditional customs observed, by the group (s.223(1)(a)); the group has a connection with the land or waters by those laws and customs (s.223(1)(b)); and the rights and interests are recognised by the common law of Australia (s.223(1)(c)).

authorities.name: Members of the Yorta Yorta Aboriginal Community v Victoria
authorities.judge_or_panel: Gleeson CJ, McHugh, Gummow, Hayne, Callinan JJ (majority, 5:2); Gaudron and Kirby JJ dissenting
authorities.proposition: Construes s.223(1)(a)'s 'traditional laws acknowledged, and traditional customs observed' requirement: the laws and customs must have their normative origin in the pre-sovereignty society, and the normative system itself must have had a continuous existence and vitality since sovereignty. Critically, the acknowledgment and observance of those laws and customs must have continued 'substantially uninterrupted' since sovereignty - though 'substantially' recognises the practical difficulty of proving continuous oral tradition over such a long period, and continuity is required of the normative system itself, not of the precise content of every law and custom, which may change over time. On the facts, the claimants' native title claim failed because 19th-century disruption meant their traditional society's laws and customs had not been substantially continuously observed.
authorities.verification_note: AustLII and Jade.io both actively blocked automated access ('access denied for AI crawlers'), confirmed by direct browser navigation, not merely WebFetch. Bibliographic details (panel, date, catchwords directly confirming engagement with s.223) were fetched directly from the High Court's own official case page. The paragraph-level holding (paras 46-48, 87-89) was corroborated by the researching agent across two independent secondary sources (a hosted full-text mirror and the Australian Law Reform Commission's official Connection to Country report), with a small residual uncertainty flagged honestly (a one-to-two paragraph spread in exactly which paragraph carries which quoted sentence). This session's own independent WebSearch further corroborated the core continuity-doctrine holding via a genuine synthesis of multiple sources, consistent with the researching agent's account.
